title: Hadamard Maximal Determinant
tagline: +1s and -1s in a grid. Maximize the determinant.
description: Fill an n x n grid with +1s and -1s. Compute the determinant. Try to beat the current record for that n. For example, for n = 23 the best known determinant is 704,643,072. Submit a 23 x 23 matrix of +1s and -1s with a larger one.
context: Hadamard asked in 1893: if every entry of a matrix is +1 or -1, how large can the determinant be? For n up to 22, the answer is known exactly after over a century of work. For n = 23 onwards, the best constructions come from hill-climbing searches run by Orrick et al. in 2003. Many of those records have stood for 20+ years. Every n in the table below is independently attackable - you pick one and try to beat it.
verification: Exact integer determinant via sympy. No floating point. Accepts if |det(M)| strictly exceeds the current record for that n.

suggestedApproach.title: Pick an n
suggestedApproach.body: Any row in the table. n = 23 is the smallest open case.

suggestedApproach.title: Random start
suggestedApproach.body: Generate a random {+1, -1} matrix. Compute its determinant.

suggestedApproach.title: Hill-climb
suggestedApproach.body: Flip entries that increase |det|. Cofactor expansion lets you update cheaply without recomputing from scratch.

suggestedApproach.title: Simulated annealing
suggestedApproach.body: Perturb when stuck. This is exactly how the 2003 records were set.

agentPrompt: I want you to find a {+1, -1} matrix of size n = 23 whose determinant (in absolute value) exceeds 704,643,072 (the current record). Use hill-climbing with simulated annealing: start from a random +/-1 matrix, repeatedly flip entries that increase |det(M)| using cofactor updates, and randomly perturb when stuck in a local maximum. Run many restarts and report the best matrix found. Output the matrix as a JSON array of arrays.

bounds.name: Hadamard bound
bounds.formula: n^(n/2). Tight when a Hadamard matrix exists.

bounds.name: Ehlich's bound
bounds.formula: Derived from eigenvalue analysis of M^T M
